clue.text: Noisy ambience for one who's challenging for title?

definitions.note: a clause describing a person; the answer is the noun for such a person

indicators.note: an ambience is what surrounds something, so the noisy word is wrapped around the one

blocks.note: clamant means loud and insistent, clamouring
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A boxer or contender bringing a loud, raucous atmosphere to a title fight.
explanation.walkthrough: CLAMANT, a rare word for clamorous, goes round I to make CLAIMANT.
explanation.definitionFit: A claimant is someone asserting a right to something, such as a throne or championship belt.

clue.text: Garden feature supporting climbers initially seen in China

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word climbers
in a down clue the supporting piece sits beneath, so the garden feature goes below

blocks.note: first letter of climbers
a rockery is a garden bed of stones and alpine plants

explanation.surface: A rock garden propping up climbing plants, as might be found in a Chinese garden.
explanation.walkthrough: China looks like the country, but it is the definition with its capital letter hiding the sense of porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: China in the sense of porcelain plates and cups is the household crockery collectively.

clue.text: Defender's collected a game point

blocks.note: taken as written
polo is a game played on horseback
the gist is the main point of something

explanation.surface: A sports defender has picked up a game point in a match.
explanation.definitionFit: An apologist is someone who argues in support of a doctrine or person, a defender of it.

clue.text: Marks on exam given in lesson

blocks.note: M abbreviates the mark, the old German currency
an oral is a spoken examination

explanation.surface: A teacher's marks on a test, handed out during class.
explanation.walkthrough: Marks looks like exam grades, but it is the old German currency, abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: The moral of a story is the lesson or teaching it is meant to convey.

clue.text: A King led astray in New York as emperor actually appeared?

indicators.note: something gone astray has wandered off course, so these letters are jumbled
in places the preceding letters inside the abbreviation for the city

blocks.note: taken as written
K is the chess abbreviation for king
the word led rearranged
the standard abbreviation for New York

explanation.surface: A monarch going the wrong way in Manhattan, followed by a question about how the emperor looked.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition alludes to the fairy tale of the Emperor's New Clothes, where the emperor paraded with nothing on.
explanation.definitionFit: In Andersen's tale the emperor's invisible clothes left him walking through the streets in the nude.

clue.text: A wild animal joining hundreds in the ark?

blocks.note: taken as written
a boar is a wild pig
D is the Roman numeral for five hundred

explanation.surface: A wild beast joining the many animals filing into Noah's ark.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is by example: on Noah's ark is one place to be on board.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in the ark means being on board a vessel, which is what the adverb describes.

clue.text: Holmes in retirement looking after workers, for example

definitions.text: Holmes in retirement looking after workers, for example

blocks.note: surface reading: the detective Sherlock Holmes after he gave up sleuthing
setter's reading: worker bees are the example, and in retirement Holmes kept hives on the Sussex Downs

explanation.surface: The great detective, now retired, supervising a team of workers.
explanation.walkthrough: Conan Doyle retired Sherlock Holmes to Sussex to keep bees; workers are worker bees, not employees.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tending hives of worker bees is an apiarist, which was Holmes's pastime after leaving Baker Street.

clue.text: Feel resentment, losing capital in low joint

indicators.note: losing its capital means the word drops its first letter

blocks.note: to rankle is to cause lasting bitterness

explanation.surface: Someone bitter about losing money in a seedy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Low joint suggests a dive or dodgy pub; it is a body joint low down on the leg.
explanation.definitionFit: The ankle is the hinge connecting the foot to the leg, the lowest major joint of the body.

clue.text: Mark making impression, comprehending Old English

indicators.note: to comprehend is literally to take in, so the impression holds the old piece

blocks.note: a dent is a hollow impression in a surface
O is the abbreviation for old
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A student's mark making an impression because they understand Anglo-Saxon.
explanation.walkthrough: Old English looks like a single unit, but only Old goes inside the dent; English follows on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To denote is to indicate or signify, as when a symbol marks out a particular thing.

clue.text: Swindle producing run on City

indicators.note: in a down clue on means placed above, so the running piece comes first

blocks.note: to flee is to run away
EC is the postcode district of the City of London, here turned round

explanation.surface: A financial fraud triggering a run on the City of London's banks.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, postal area EC; the clue gives no signal for turning it round, so this looks like a loose clue.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece someone is to cheat them out of money, stripping them as a sheep is shorn.

clue.text: Stench from continental river, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells us the river's name is only to be spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: the Oder flows between Germany and Poland; in British speech it is said like the word for a smell

explanation.surface: A bad smell rising from a river on the Continent.
explanation.definitionFit: An odour is a smell, and especially in the plural or with context an unpleasant one.

clue.text: Like drink fermented in its container

indicators.note: fermenting stirs and changes a brew, so these letters are reworked

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Beer, say, fermenting in the vessel that holds it.
explanation.walkthrough: A kilderkin is an old cask size, half a barrel, used for beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A small cask holding about eighteen gallons is a vessel for beer, the drink just mentioned.

clue.text: Book end and shelf retaining current information

indicators.note: end points to the final letter of book
retaining means holding on to, so the first pair of pieces keeps the third within it

blocks.note: last letter of book
a ledge is a narrow shelf
current in the sense of present-day, happening now

explanation.surface: A bookend and a bookshelf in a library holding up-to-date reference works.
explanation.walkthrough: Book end is not a bookend but the end letter of book; current is not electricity but the present.
explanation.definitionFit: Knowledge is facts and learning acquired, which is to say information one holds.

clue.text: Give a seat to person who's standing

definitions.text: Give a seat to person who's standing

blocks.clueFragment: Give a seat to person who's standing
blocks.note: surface reading: being polite on a crowded bus or train
setter's reading: voters handing a parliamentary seat to a candidate who stands at the polls

explanation.surface: Offering your seat on the bus to a passenger left on their feet.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a candidate stands for Parliament and the winner takes a seat in the House of Commons.
explanation.definitionFit: Voters choose a candidate for office by ballot, which puts them into a parliamentary seat.

clue.text: Approach following distress is on right lines

indicators.note: following tells us the approach comes after the distress

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
to ail is to trouble or afflict
a way in the sense of a method or approach

explanation.surface: Someone in trouble being told their method is on the right track.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue, A on B puts A after B, so the right abbreviation leads.
explanation.definitionFit: Railway lines are the tracks trains run on, so lines here means the permanent way.

clue.text: Misdirected infantry put off balance

blocks.note: something misdirected has gone the wrong way
foot soldiers are the infantry

explanation.surface: Foot soldiers sent the wrong way and thrown into disarray.
explanation.definitionFit: To wrong-foot an opponent is to catch them unprepared, as a tennis player is caught leaning the other way.

clue.text: Perish in rough water ebbing in river

indicators.note: ebbing water flows back out, so the word runs backwards
in puts the turned word inside the river

blocks.note: the Exe is a river in Devon
a rip is a stretch of turbulent water

explanation.surface: Someone drowning in choppy water as the tide goes out.
explanation.walkthrough: Rough water is a rip, a turbulent current, not a description of the river.
explanation.definitionFit: To expire is to die, a formal synonym for perish.

clue.text: Scholar putting dress on to take part in elaborate ceremony

indicators.note: in a down clue putting something on another sets it above, so dress comes first

blocks.note: rig is clothing, an outfit
a Master of Arts, a graduate scholar
a role is a part in a play

explanation.surface: An academic in gown dressing up to play a role in a grand ritual.
explanation.definitionFit: A rigmarole is a lengthy, complicated procedure, a palaver of fuss and formality.

clue.text: Joined in operation, and longed to get under way

indicators.note: in a down clue going under means being placed below the other piece

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
to itch for something is to long for it

explanation.surface: A surgeon keen to get the operation started.
explanation.walkthrough: Under way reads as started, but way is the street abbreviation that the longing sits beneath.
explanation.definitionFit: A surgeon closes a wound by sewing it, so edges joined during an operation are sutured.

clue.text: Walked in wild parts of Dorset

indicators.note: wild parts suggests the pieces of the county name are scattered and disordered

blocks.note: the county name taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A hiker tramping across Dorset's untamed countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: Dorset is a rural county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Strode is the past tense of stride, to walk with long purposeful steps.

clue.text: Whole lot of conservationists in Ireland

indicators.note: in places the conservation body inside the country

blocks.note: Eire is the Irish name for Ireland
the National Trust, the British heritage charity, abbreviated

explanation.surface: A whole crowd of environmentalists gathering in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Whole lot looks like one phrase, but Whole is the definition and lot of conservationists is the National Trust, which preserves British historic houses and land.
explanation.definitionFit: Entire means complete, with no part missing, the same as whole.

clue.text: Erect and riding with authority

blocks.note: a jockey who is up is riding a horse
a right is an entitlement or authority to act

explanation.surface: A rider sitting tall and commanding in the saddle.
explanation.walkthrough: In racing a jockey is said to be up when mounted, as in 'with Smith up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Upright means standing vertically, straight up, which is what erect means as an adjective.

clue.text: Get lift from university honour

definitions.note: the phrase means raise up; the answer is the verb to raise up

blocks.note: U is the abbreviation for university
to honour someone is to praise them

explanation.surface: A graduate's spirits boosted by an academic award.
explanation.definitionFit: To upraise something is an old verb for hoisting or elevating it higher.

clue.text: Sticker to permit entry by one member

indicators.note: entry means going in, so one member is admitted inside the permit word

blocks.note: to let is to allow
the Roman numeral for one
a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A parking or entry sticker permitting one club member to get in.
explanation.walkthrough: Sticker suggests a label; it is the shellfish that clings to rocks.
explanation.definitionFit: A limpet clamps itself to rocks so firmly that it is a byword for anything that clings on.

clue.text: Under cover. US soldier gets back without officer

indicators.note: back says the soldier's abbreviation is read from right to left
without in its old sense of outside, so the soldier goes around the officer

blocks.note: GI is slang for an American soldier
a non-commissioned officer

explanation.surface: An American GI returning secretly from a mission without their commanding officer.
explanation.walkthrough: Without reads as lacking, but here it means outside; the full stop marks the definition as an abbreviated word.
explanation.definitionFit: Incog is a shortening of incognito, meaning with one's identity concealed.

clue.text: Bit of the joint that's put in dish

blocks.note: a cut is a piece of a joint of meat
ie abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: A piece of the roast placed on a serving plate.
explanation.walkthrough: Dish reads as a plate, but it is slang for an attractive person.
explanation.definitionFit: Dish is informal for a good-looking person, and a cutie is likewise an attractive one.

clue.text: What could be matter with nag like this?

definitions.text: What could be matter with nag like this?

indicators.note: what could be invites us to imagine the letters forming something else

blocks.note: the two words matter and nag, joined by with

explanation.surface: Asking what is wrong with a scolding person who behaves like this.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: a nag like this is the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A termagant is a shrewish, bullying woman, the sort who nags relentlessly.

clue.text: Dismay produced by attraction out East

indicators.note: out means removed, so the compass point is taken away

blocks.note: appeal is the power to attract
E is the abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: Being dismayed by the allure of the Orient.
explanation.definitionFit: To appal is to shock or horrify, filling someone with dismay.

clue.text: Our trip out on river something of a mixture

indicators.note: out suggests the trip has gone awry, so its letters are disordered
in an across clue on means added after, so the river comes first

blocks.note: the Po is Italy's longest river
the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A boating outing on a river that turned out a mixed experience.
explanation.definitionFit: A potpourri is a mixed bowl of dried petals, and by extension any medley or miscellany.

clue.text: Dog caught in bear hug

indicators.note: to hug is to wrap one's arms around, so the bear encloses the caught letter

blocks.note: Winnie-the-Pooh, the famous bear of A. A. Milne
C is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: A dog trapped in the crushing embrace of a bear.
explanation.walkthrough: Bear hug reads as one squeeze, but bear is the Milne character and hug does the enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: Pooch is a jocular slang term for a dog.

clue.text: Bargains in entertainments

blocks.note: first meaning: negotiates, as in treating with an enemy
second meaning: special pleasures or outings laid on for someone

explanation.surface: Cheap deals to be had on shows and amusements.
explanation.walkthrough: Bargains looks like a noun for good deals; it is the verb, to negotiate terms.
explanation.definitionFit: To treat with someone is to negotiate terms, and a treat is a pleasure or outing provided for others.

clue.text: Fit to study, being bookish

blocks.note: fit in the sense of healthy, well
to read a subject is to study it at university

explanation.surface: Someone healthy enough to study, and studious by nature.
explanation.definitionFit: A well-read person has read widely and is learned, much as a bookish person loves books.
